label: rem:spatial-realization-base-generality
title: The base of the spatial realisation: the properties used and the case excluded
html:
The spatial realisation functor states that its target M = \mathrm{Spec}(A) is an ordinary smooth manifold. That is an assertion of the definition, not a consequence of the axioms, and it is worth separating the two: which properties of M the constructions of this paper use, and which are decoration.

What is used. Four properties, each a property of the algebra A in \mathbf{C} rather than of a manifold.

  1. The points. M is the set of categorical points p \colon \mathbf{1} \to A, and the local germ A/\mathfrak{m}_{p}^{2} \cong \mathbf{1} \oplus \mathfrak{m}_{p}/\mathfrak{m}_{p}^{2} at p is Zariski's description of a tangent space; it makes sense for any commutative algebra and gives a vector space of constant dimension exactly when A is regular.
  2. The one-forms. The module \Omega^{1}(A) of Kähler differentials exists by hypothesis, and the constructions use that \tau(\Omega^{1}(A)) is the module of sections of a bundle — that is, that \Omega^{1}(A) is a dualisable object of \mathbf{C} of constant rank. For a finitely generated algebra over a field, \Omega^{1}(A) finitely generated projective of rank \dim A is equivalent to smoothness [hartshorne-1977]; it is the same hypothesis under which the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg theorem identifies Hochschild homology with differential forms [hkr-1962].
  3. The contact form \varTheta_{A}, which needs only \Omega^{1}(A), the Frobenius form and the universal derivation.
  4. The Reeb derivation, which needs a torus action and the contraction \iota_{\xi} on \Omega^{1}(A).

Nothing uses a topology on M, a partition of unity, or the real numbers.

What can therefore replace "smooth manifold". Any base on which \Omega^{1}(A) is dualisable of constant rank: a smooth affine variety over a field, which is the case of the finite-field models of a later section of this chapter; a formal scheme, when A is completed at a point; a smooth rigid-analytic space, for the p-adic models; a supermanifold, when A is \mathbb{Z}/2-graded; or a quotient stack [M/G] when A carries the action of a finite group such as the S_{5} of Bring's curve, in which case the categorical points of the invariant subalgebra are the orbits. The proofs of this chapter go through verbatim in each case, because they never leave the category \mathbf{C}. The word "manifold" fixes the real-analytic case for the reader and is the case in which the physical interpretation is made; it is not what the theorems require.

The singular base. The one case the constructions exclude is a base whose Kähler module fails to be projective. The affine cone over Bring's curve is such a base: away from the vertex it is smooth, but at the vertex the fibre of \mathfrak{m}_{p}/\mathfrak{m}_{p}^{2} jumps to the dimension of the ambient space, \Omega^{1} is not locally free, and the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg identification fails. The link of that vertex — the boundary of a small neighbourhood of it — is a three-manifold fibred by circles over the curve with Euler number 2 - 2g = -6 [orlik-wagreich1971], whose fundamental group is infinite; a quaternionic model of the cone describes the smooth fibre near a point of the curve, not this link. The phrase "ordinary smooth manifold" therefore has a single function in the definition: it excludes the vertex. Stated as the categorical condition, that exclusion is a checkable hypothesis, and the generality of the previous paragraph follows without further work.
